s0.why: [42] defines a plate boundary as where two plates meet; [6] says relative motion sets the type: convergent, divergent or transform.

s1.why: [10] gives subduction into the mantle at convergent boundaries; [11]-[12] give new crust by seafloor spreading keeping total area constant.

s2.why: [43] lists earthquakes and the creation of mountains, volcanoes, mid-ocean ridges and oceanic trenches at plate boundaries.

f1.why: [7] says relative movement typically ranges from zero to 10 cm annually.

f2.why: [44] calls the Pacific plate's Ring of Fire the most active of the boundary volcano zones.

f3.why: [39] gives about 6 km at mid-ocean ridges to greater than 100 km at subduction zones.

q1.why: [10] places subduction, one plate edge carried under the other into the mantle, along convergent boundaries.

q2.why: [10]-[11] say subduction reduces surface area and [12] says spreading balances it, the conveyor belt.

q3.why: [44] says the vast majority of active volcanoes occur along plate boundaries; [45] says only some are in plate interiors.

q4.why: [35],[38] make thickness a function of age and distance from the ridge; [39] gives 6 km at the ridge, the minimum.

q5.why: [27] gives 10 to 40 mm a year at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, about as fast as fingernails grow.

q6.why: [32] says oceanic crust is denser than continental; [19] says cold, dense oceanic crust sinks into the mantle at subduction zones.

b0.why: [10]-[12] give subduction balancing spreading with constant area; [18] backs the feedback that cooling raises density.

b1.why: [10] pairs convergent with a plate going down, [12] divergent margins with new crust by spreading, [39] the 6 km and over 100 km thicknesses.

b2.why: [38] gives forming at the ridge and spreading out, [36]-[37] cooling then cooled mantle added to the base, [39] travel until subduction at over 100 km.

b3.why: [30] and [31] give the two modes of formation, [32] oceanic is denser, [33] oceanic below and continental above sea level.
